content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper develops Noether Embeddings, an embedding method that is designed to help efficiently discover the same causes and effects that exhibit similar durations in  temporal knowledge graphs, e.g., when B declares war on A, A reduces diplomatic relations in 2 days with B.  These relationships are known as temporal associations. The approach is inspired by Noether’s theorem from physics, and is centered on learning complex embeddings of event quadruples with the goal of mapping cause and effect pairs to similar vectors. This makes finding common cause and effect pairs (that exhibit similar durations) efficient. In experiments, the proposed embeddings are tested for speed and accuracy of querying for temporal associations. The results show that the proposed method achieves higher query accuracy than other embedding approaches (that are not designed for temporal associate mining), but lower accuracy than optimized search. However, the embedding method is many times more efficient than the optimized search approach.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Novelty of the connection between Noether’s theorem to temporal association mining as well as its application to a problem of interest.
- Empirical and theoretical results are provided for the proposed embedding method.
- Empirical results show that the proposed approach is many times faster than existing methods (ignoring the cost of computing the embeddings).

Weaknesses:
- One motivation for the work is that temporal knowledge graphs are constantly growing and evolving with event regularities also changing, which requires efficient temporal association mining. But as far as I understand, Noether Embeddings must be re-computed after each batch of new data. Since the cost of computing Noether Embeddings isn’t discussed, it’s difficult to know if Noether embeddings is a practical solution to handling constantly growing data, or if encoding the quadruples is too costly.
- Being unfamiliar with Noether’s theorem, I found many aspects of this paper unclear.
- Empirical results show that Noether embeddings help speed up search for temporal associations at the cost of accuracy. However, there is no discussion of the actual time it takes to run the optimized search or search with Noether embeddings (just the relative speed) so it is unclear whether the speed-for-accuracy tradeoff is worthwhile.
- The authors claim that finding TAs can expand human understanding of regularities in events, but only 2 patterns of real world events are presented in a case study. Are there any other patterns discovered that are more surprising? Since it is my understanding that Noether Embeddings only help with discovering TAs quickly, better evidence of the importance of this task should be supplied.

content.title: First Part of Response
content.comment:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer for spending valuable time on reviewing our manuscript and providing insightful comments. We have improved our work to a large extent with the guide of the reviewer’s comments. Responses are as below.

## Major Improvements
1. We have clarified the presentations in the manuscript.
2. We have extended an online TAM experiment to demonstrate the practicality and potential of our method further.
3. We have extended NE for querying arbitrary event pairs, have given a more general version of the theoretical proof, and have conducted relevant experiments.
4. We have further proposed a general heuristic embedding construction procedure with Noether’s theorem.
5. We have developed a unified NE, which is both theoretically provable and experimentally efficient, and have renewed relevant experiments.
6. We have conducted experiments with 3 more non-trivial TKG baselines to show the necessity of our embedding model.

## Heuristic construction by Noether’s theorem
Noether’s theorem states that symmetries correspond to conservation laws. Meanwhile, any meaning information in an axiomatized physical system can be deductively derived once its action is constructed, including Noether’s theorem.

We aim to construct an embedding model of TKG quadruples that naturally contains the inductive bias of time translation symmetry and can be decoded for searching conserved quantities. However, the construction of such an embedding model and its decoding function is without a guide, and therefore hard. 

Analogizing a zero-mass two-particle system connected by a spring, we therefore deduct from only a constructed action to get meaningful inspirations for constructing Noether Embeddings. We summarize the procedure into 5 processes: (1) construction of action (by analogizing a physical system with similar symmetries); (2)applying Euler-Lagrange Equation; (3)applying transformation of symmetry; (4)combining conclusions from (2) and (3) to derive the conserved quantity and constraints for embedding construction; (5)getting inspirations. This procedure can be extended to explore the regularities of other symmetries.

## Key technical innovation (why NE works)

The key technical innovation of NE is the specific use of a global rotating complex vector $r(t)$ for an EFFICIENT inverse cross-correlation-like query of temporal associations by encoding the time translation symmetry of TAs. In the encoding process, $r(t)$ conducts a Fourier expansion of time while training each event embeddings $q(t)=u \circ r(t)$. The decoding process (calculating $g(\tau)$) only requires a RELATIVE time range ($\tau\ _r$), regardless of the absolute time of relevant events across time($t\in T_a$). This is caused by the fact that $g(\tau)=||u_c-u_e \circ r(\tau)||=||u_c \circ r(t)-u_e \circ r(t+\tau)||=||q_c(t)-q_e(t+\tau)||$ for any $t$. Relevant event pairs across time (‘for any $t$’) are therefore automatically ‘gathered’ and ‘averaged’ when learning each event embeddings to form the same $g(\tau)$, due to the time translation symmetry of TAs introduced by $r(t)$. This enables TAQ to be conducted efficiently by calculating $g(\tau)$ in a minor time complexity. 

## Illustration of the mining framework
1. Encoding. The inputs are structured events, such as (s,p,o,t) quadruples. The
outputs are complex vectors, including entities, predicates, and a global time vector of $\omega$. The encoding process can be implemented in batches or streams, because the most minor component of a training loss is only relevant to the specific information of a single event. The event embeddings, score function, and loss function are concerned in the encoding stage.
2. Decoding. The inputs are trained complex vectors and TA queries of
$(s,o,p_c,p_e)$. The outputs are decoding results, computed by the decoding function $g(\tau)$ and further redistributed by the converting function $p(\tau)$ to form an approximate probability distribution of relative time. $\tau$ is traversed in an arbitrary queried range of relative time points, such as $\tau \in T_r=\\{0,1,2,…,30\\}$, which can be different from the collection of absolute time points, such as $t \in T_a=\\{0,1,…,365\\}$. The maximum of $p(\tau)$ is then derived. Note that no training is included in this process, which only requires inference of trained vectors. The decoding and converting functions are concerned in the decoding stage.
3. Selecting. The inputs are the decoding results of each TA query. The outputs are 
the judgement of each TA query. A global threshold $p_{th}$ is set, compared with the maximum of $p(\tau)$ for judgements. Once the maximum exceeds $p_{th}$, a TA is justified as exists and the corresponding $\tau$ that maximizes $p(\tau)$ is selected. Computations in this stage are conducted one-by-one for fair comparison with Search.

## References
[1] Namaki et al., Discovering Graph Temporal Association Rules, CIKM 2017.

content.title: Second Part of Response
content.comment:
## Point-to-Point Responses
### Weaknesses
> Q1: it’s difficult to know if Noether embeddings is a practical solution to handling constantly growing data, or if encoding the quadruples is too costly

A1: Yes, it is. The encoding time can be ignored so long as it is consistent with the update period of the event stream. 
In the case of online ICEWS14, the update period is 24h which is essentially larger than the training time of 2.2, 2.9, 5.4, and 6.8 seconds over one batch. Note that the encoding time of batches on the fly can be largely reduced than the cold start batch. Meanwhile, NE has also mined massive TAs whose relative time is larger than the batch window in stream processing scenarios, while Search cannot, which is also demonstrated by experiments. Details of the newly conducted experiments can be seen in ‘Results in online settings’ in Section 5.2.


> Q2: Being unfamiliar with Noether’s theorem, I found many aspects of this paper unclear.

A2: We have greatly improved our expressions in the manuscript. The key idea is summarized in ‘Heuristic construction by Noether’s theorem’ above.

> Q3: However, there is no discussion of the actual time it takes to run the optimized search or search with Noether embeddings (just the relative speed) so it is unclear whether the speed-for-accuracy tradeoff is worthwhile

A3: The same as A1 in ‘Weaknesses’ (and A8 in ‘Clarity’).

> Q4: but only 2 patterns of real world events are presented in a case study. Are there any other patterns discovered that are more surprising?

A4: Yes, there are. We present here another two TAs mined from ICEWS18: (1) Whenever Donald Trump discusses by telephone with China, then in around 24 days, he will consider policy option to China. (2) Syria will provide military protection or peacekeeping to Turkey back in around two days whenever Syria fights with artillery and tanks against Turkey.
Since NE can be extended to explore temporal associations with more relaxed forms, such as $p_1(s_1,o_1,t) \to p_2(s_2,o_2,t+\bigtriangleup) \quad \forall t \in T_a$ and $p_1(s_1,t) \to p_2(s_2,t+\bigtriangleup) \forall t \in T_a$, we report relevant cases in Appendix C.


### Clarity-1
> Q1: However, are there no indexing schemes and/or parallel algorithms for temporal associate mining? Online index structures might have the added benefit of not needing costly updates when new data arrives.’

A1: Fundamentally, almost all representation learning algorithms can be converted to a search algorithm. Namaki CIKM 2017[1] is a classic algorithm that implements an optimized search method for graph temporal association mining. Unlike the search method in that case, where a fixed relative time has to be set for TAM (such as $\tau=5$), NE allows the direct fitting and plotting of an approximate probability distribution of relative time within the queried range. With the three-stage framework, the major time complexity of TAM is also rearranged into the encoding process, where the training time of NE can be ignored as long as it is shorter than the update period of event stream.

> Q2: TA: please clarify “width proportional to its mean”.

A2: $ \bigtriangleup=\bigtriangleup (\eta)=[\tau(1-\eta), \tau(1+\eta)] $, where relative time $\tau$ is the mean of relative interval $\bigtriangleup $ whose width is $2\tau\eta$.

> Q3: Are the ranges of sc and hc between 0 and 1? If so, what is the range of gc? In the end of Section 2.1, the claim is that gc \in [0,1].

A3: Yes, their potential range is both $[0,1]$. 

> Q4: In Section 2.2: what is a center point, \delta(\eta)

A4: The center point of $\bigtriangleup (\eta)=[\tau(1-\eta), \tau(1+\eta)]$ is $\tau$.

> Q5: In Section 2.2, what does the notation (s, p_c, o, t) \in (s, p_e, o, t_\delta) mean? I don’t think this notation has been introduced before

A5: This means that whenever $s$ conduct $p_c$ to $o$, $s$ will further conduct $p_e$ to $o$ in a relative interval of $\bigtriangleup$.

content.title: Third Part of Response
content.comment:
### Clarity-2

> Q6: In Figure 1: please define a “good” and “bad” TA.

A6: Good TAs are those with high gcs, while bad TAs are those with low gcs. The decoding results in our framework can be used to approximate gcs.

> Q7: In the results reported in Table 2: is NE-A on GPU compared to Search on GPU or CPU? Has Search been optimized for GPU? Also, what are the raw times?

A7: In the TAM experiment, Search is implemented on a cpu; the encoding and decoding stage of NE is implemented on a gpu; the selecting stage is on a cpu, the same as Search. The raw time of Search in TAM on ICEWS14, ICEWS18, and GDELT is 17.9s, 74.2s, and 7135s, respectively.

> Q8: What is the training time required for Noether Embeddings? How does it compare to query time for Search and other algorithms?

A8: The training time of NE on ICEWS14 of TAQ is 25.8s, with event num=5. The query time of Search with 1000 queries under the same settings is 3.1s.
Though training time is relatively great compared to Search, it can be ignored in online settings (details in Section 5.2), so pure query time or mining time is what matters.

> Q9: Given that new temporal data is always being added, how often do Noether embeddings need to be retrained with new data? Is this practical?

A9: The same as A1 in ‘Weaknesses’(and A8 in ‘Clarity’).

> Q10: Equation 8 defines the function h to be the Hadamard product of s,p,o and r. But then in equation 9, the score function computes the norm of a difference of h and the Hadamard product, which by 8 I believe are equal. What am I missing here? Then q(s,p,ot) seems to also be defined as the Hadamard product of s,p,o, and r. I find this confusing.

A10: Yes, they were somewhat equal. We replace event embeddings for the original mapping function in the latest version of the manuscript, where the definition of the score function uses the definition of event embeddings, and the definition of the loss function uses the information of the score function.

> Q11: Please write down a single theorem statement (Section 5.1). Also, please explain the theorem statement in language.

A11: Two conclusions can be drawn from the theorems. First is convergence. Conserved quantities of $g(\tau)$ will be promised if the loss is trained towards zero. Second is competition. Considering all the sample pairs of the same relative time of $\tau$ for a potential TA. The pair that are both positive or both negative samples makes $g(\tau)$ small, while the pair where one is positive and the other one is negative makes $g(\tau)$ big. Therefore, the inverse of $g(\tau)$ plots an approximate cross-correlation function of $\tau$. 

> Q12: To what does equation 13 refer?

A12: In our latest version of the manuscript, we construct a single and final NE to replace NE-O and NE-A, which is both theoretically reasonable and experimentally efficient.

> Q13: How is query accuracy computed (with increasing number of event pairs)?

A13: The overall accuracy = number of correct queries / number of total queries.
For a query $(s,o,p_c,p_e)$, given the setting parameter $\eta$ which determines the width of a $\bigtriangleup=[\tau(1-\eta), \tau(1+\eta)]$: if the query is not a TA then an answer of $-1$ is expected; else a correct $\tau$ needs to be selected, that falls into the ground truth $\bigtriangleup$. Detailed illustrations can be found in Section 2.2 and Appendix B.2.1.


> Q14: Figure 5 is confusing, perhaps because I do not think there is a definition of “good” vs. “bad” TAs. Instead of showing that the curves are different, is there an experiment where distinction between good and bad TAs is demonstrated?

A14: A TA with high gc is defined as good, while that of low gc is defined as bad. In the latest version of the experiment, we compare the extreme cases of two decoding results that $gc_1=1$ and $gc_2=0$.

> Q15: How are hyperparameters (gc, sp, etc.) chosen?

A15: For hyperparameters of models: we use hyperparameter settings in the corresponding papers for baselines. Hyperparameters and thresholds of NE are tuned over grid search. Detailed information can be found in Appendix C.
$gc_l, sp_l$ can be regarded as the task setting of TAM. For hyperparameters of task settings: $gc \geq 0.7, sp \geq 2$ is a reasonable standard of a TA being ‘confident’ and ‘reliable’.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Inspired by Noether's Theorem, the submission proposes an efficient mining framework for temporal association mining (TAM). The constructed embedding model allows the direct decoding of temporal associations between event pairs. The decodable model is then used to accelerate TA Querying and TAM. The authors empirically find that the proposed framework is efficient on TAQ and TAM datasets. Furthermore, from the theoretical side, the authors proved the model enforces convergence to a conserved quantity of decoding results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. Two new tasks are proposed, namely, Temporal Aossication Querying (TAQ) and Temporal Association Mining (TAM) on Temporal Knowledge Graphs. Some interesting metrics are also designed for these tasks.

2. A new model is proposed. It contains encoding, decoding, and selecting with our developed framework.

3. It has been proved that the embedding model enforces the convergence to a conserved quantity.

Weakness:
1. The technical novelty of the proposed framework is limited. 1) Theorem 1 is trivial (especially the proof) under some strong assumptions. The validation of applying theorem 1 to the proposed method is not properly justified. How these assumptions are reasonable to the problem settings? 2) The idea of using Noether's theorem is not new to the AI field. The only new part is applying Noether's theorem to do some mining tasks on temporal knowledge graphs.

2. The challenges of proposed tasks TAQ and TAM on temporal graphs are unclear. It would be helpful if the authors could elaborate challenges of these tasks.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The submission proposes an efficient mining framework for temporal association mining (TAM). The constructed embedding model allows the direct decoding of temporal associations between event pairs. The decodable model is then used to accelerate TA Querying and TAM. The authors empirically find that the proposed framework is efficient on TAQ and TAM datasets. Furthermore, from the theoretical side, the authors proved the model enforces convergence to a conserved quantity of decoding results. The presentation of this paper is clear. However, it is unclear whether the authors will publish the code and datasets.

See the overall review below.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, this submission proposes some new tasks and a framework for temporal association-related tasks. The idea of applying using Noether's Theorem is interesting. However, the overall novelty is limited. The proof of the Theorem seems trivial (e.g., only triangle inequalities are used). Furthermore, this theorem and the proof do not tell the reviewer any meaningful information. The authors make some strong assumptions but do not justify whether these assumptions are reasonable. We would like to sincerely appreciate the reviewer for spending valuable time reviewing our manuscript and providing insightful comments. Responses are as below.

## Major Improvements
1. We have clarified the presentations in the manuscript.
2. We have extended NE for querying event pairs of arbitrary event types, have given a more general version of the theoretical proof, and have conducted relevant experiments.
3. We have further proposed a general heuristic embedding construction procedure with Noether’s theorem.
4. We have developed a unified NE, which is both theoretically provable and experimentally efficient, and have renewed relevant experiments.
5. We have conducted experiments with three more non-trivial TKG baselines (including TeRo Xu. Et al. [1]) to show the necessity of our embedding model.
6. We have extended an online TAM experiment to demonstrate the practicality and potential of our method further.

## Novelty of significance
1. Embedding. We develop an embedding model NE of structured events that naturally encodes the time translation symmetry of TAs, and can efficiently decode conserved quantities to query TAs.
2. Mining. We develop a TAM framework that (1) supports efficient query of an approximate probability distribution of the relative time points within an arbitrary queried range of a potential TA, and (2) rearranges the major time complexity of TAM into the encoding stage, where the training time of NE can be ignored as long as it is shorter than the update period of the event stream.
3. Noether. We develop a heuristic embedding construction procedure, where axiomatized physical systems that satisfy Noether’s theorem can aid the discovery of regularities with general symmetries.


## Key technical innovation (why NE works)
The key technical innovation of NE is the specific use of a global rotating complex vector $r(t)$ for an EFFICIENT cross-correlation-like query of temporal associations by encoding the time translation symmetry of TAs. In the encoding process, $r(t)$ conducts a Fourier expansion for a series of the event embeddings $q(t)=u \circ r(t)$ of each event type while training. The decoding process (calculating $g(\tau)$) only requires a RELATIVE time range ($\tau\in T_r$), regardless of the absolute time of relevant events across time($t\in T_a$). This is caused by the fact that $g(\tau)=||u_c-u_e \circ r(\tau)||=||u_c \circ r(t)-u_e \circ r(t+\tau)||=||q_c(t)-q_e(t+\tau)||$ for any $t$. Relevant event pairs across time (‘for any $t$’) are therefore automatically ‘gathered’ and ‘averaged’ when learning each event embeddings to form the same $g(\tau)$, due to the time translation symmetry of TAs introduced by $r(t)$. This enables TAQ to be conducted efficiently by calculating $g(\tau)$ in minor time complexity. 


## References
[1] Xu et al., TeRo: A Time-aware Knowledge Graph Embedding via Temporal Rotation, ACL 2020.

[2] Namaki et al., Discovering Graph Temporal Association Rules, CIKM 2017.

content.title: Second Part of Response
content.comment:
## Point-to-Point Responses
> Q1: However, it is unclear whether the authors will publish the code and datasets

A1: The code and datasets will be made public and have previously been included in ‘supplementary material’. The updated code and datasets will be submitted in the revised version.

> Q2: The proof of the Theorem seems trivial (e.g., only triangle inequalities are used)’ & ‘This theorem and the proof do not tell the reviewer any meaningful information

A2: Two conclusions can be drawn from the theorems. First is convergence. Conserved quantities of $g(\tau)$ will be promised if the loss is trained towards zero. Second is competition. Considering all the sample pairs of the same relative time of $\tau$ for a potential TA. The pair that are both positive or both negative samples makes $g(\tau)$ small, while the pair where one is positive and the other one is negative makes $g(\tau)$ big. Therefore, the inverse of $g(\tau)$ plots an approximate cross-correlation function of $\tau$. 

> Q3: The only new part is applying Noether's theorem to do some mining tasks on temporal knowledge graphs

A3: Noether’s theorem states that symmetries correspond to conservation laws. Meanwhile, any meaning information in an axiomatized physical system can be deductively derived once its action is constructed, including Noether’s theorem.
We aim to construct an embedding model that naturally encodes the time translation symmetry of TAs, and a corresponding decoding function $g(\tau)$ that only requires traversing through a fixed range of relative time points $\tau\in T_r$ to query each TA.
However, the construction of such an embedding model and its decoding function is without a guide, and therefore hard. 
Analogizing a zero-mass two-particle system connected by a spring, we therefore deduct from only a constructed action to get meaningful inspirations for constructing Noether Embeddings. We summarize the procedure into 5 processes: (1)construction of action (by analogizing a physical system with similar symmetries); (2)applying Euler-Lagrange Equation; (3)applying transformation of symmetry; (4)combining conclusions from (2) and (3) to derive the conserved quantity and constraints for embedding construction; (5)getting inspirations. This procedure can be extended to aid the exploration of regularities with general symmetries.

> Q4: The authors make some strong assumptions but do not justify whether these assumptions are reasonable.

A4: In our latest version of proof, theorem 1: $g(\tau) < \frac{2\eta}{\sqrt{d}c_1}$, theorem 2:$g(\tau) > \frac{|C_p-C_n|-2\eta}{\sqrt{d}c_2}$. For quantities above, $ \eta $ can be directly controlled by the training loss; $C_p$ and $C_n$ are artificially set constants. The distribution of values in the time vector $\omega$ and the ratio of the number of sample pairs and vector dimensions jointly result in the fact that $ c_1>0, c_2>0 $ in most circumstances. Details are updated in Section 4.2 and Appendix A.

> Q5: The challenges of proposed tasks TAQ and TAM on temporal graphs are unclear. It would be helpful if the authors could elaborate challenges of these tasks.

A5: Primarily, the O(N) time complexity and the large data volume of TKGs jointly result in computing difficulties. Taking GDELT as an example, a Google-made social sensor monitors the whole world and updates thousands of global events every 15 minutes [1]. Larger TKGs are being constructed in our fast growing big data era. It is far from satisfactory if we have to compute by a time complexity linear to the number of relevant events of a potential TA for efficient TAQ on such TKGs. Besides, the heterogeneous characteristics of semantic space and time in (s, p, o, t) quadruples demand a unified processing framework.


## References
[1] Leetaru and Schrodt, Gdelt: Global data on events, location, and tone, 1979–2012, ISA annual convention 2013.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
(__This review is provided based on an emergency review request.__)
* This paper propose an approach to mine temporally adjacent quadruple (subject, relation, object, timestamp) pairs in temporal knowledge graphs, such that the quadruple pair is significant according to certain statistical measures. 
* Claiming the search space used in exact search being "enormous", this paper proposed to first embed the quadruple into d-dimensional vector space, and then conduct search over the vector space. More specifically, the quadruples are embedded close to the Hadamard product of the corresponding subject and object entity, regardless of the relation and timestamp embeddings. By contrasting a quadruple embedding with negative samples (quadruples with randomly swapped entities), entities that frequently appear in the data will be embedded close to each other and vice versa. This enables the distances in the embedding space to serve as a proxy for the "associativity" in the combinatorial search space. This approach is termed NE-O. The paper also provide interesting analogy to the Noether theorem.
* Claiming the NE-O is still inefficient, an approximation that uses the loss function proposed in TNTCompLEX (Lacroix et. al. 2020 [1]) to train the embedding, and keep the same similarity measure (Eq. 11) for search. This approach is termed NE-A. All experiments conducted afterwords are based on NE-A.
* Experimental results shows the proposed NE-A achieves 90% temporal association query accuracy on semi-synthetic dataset, while exact search is 100%, and a nontrivial baseline (TNTComplEX) performs nearly random 50%. Empirical results also shows on both temporal association query and mining task, the NE-A approach is faster comparing to the exact search. Two examples of the minded patterns are also given as an illustration.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
* The temporal association mining is an interesting problem.
* The analogy between the proposed approach and Noether theorem is interesting.
* Empirical evaluation shows the proposed approximation NE-A is more efficient in finding significant temporally adjacent quadruples than exact search. The evaluation also shows NE-A is more effective than TNTComplEX (under the specific usage described in B2) in search accuracy on semi-synthetic data.

### Weakness
* **[clarity] The paper is poorly presented**. 
	* The the search procedure that how in NE-A method embedding similarity is used to efficiently find relevant quadruple pairs and prune irrelevant ones is not clearly described. In section 4, decoding phase, only the similarity measure (Eq. 11) is introduced, but no search procedure is mentioned (e.g. could be similar to Algorithm 1, yet perhaps using kNN search instead). Lacking such description makes presented NE-A method incomplete and thus difficult to assess. Also the embeddings learned according to Eq. 9 and Eq. 11 are potentially not capable of encoding the temporal order (as they are ignored in function $h$), understanding the search and filtering procedure is crucial to assess the soundness of the paper.
	* many notations are used without definition or clarification, which makes the presented ideas difficult to grasp.			
		* Above Eq. 6, notation $X(q,t)$ and $\Phi(q, t)$ are not defined.
		* Eq. 9, function $h$ only depend on $s$ and $o$ (why not $p$ or $r(t)$) is not motivated. 
		* Eq. 10, $\gamma$ is not defined
		* Eq. 11, $\tau$ is defined as relative interval, however on page 2, the notation $T$  is also referred to as relative interval, could it be the set of all possible relative intervals (as this concepts appeared in Appendix Algorithm 1 and never used in the main text)? 
		* Eq. 11, as $\tau$ is an interval, $t$  is a timestamp, it is unclear how to understand condition $t\to\tau$. Also under the same reasoning, should the $r(t)$ in Eq. 11 be $r(\tau)$? then $r(\tau)$ is also not yet defined...
		* Eq. 13, the upper limit of $i$ is $n$, which is not defined.

* **[novelty] The novelty and significance of the proposed approach is limited.**
	* Comparing to graph temporal association rule mining Namaki CIKM 2017 [2], where two temporally adjacent subgraphs (arbitrary but with bounded node cardinality) are searched, in this paper, only fixed quadruple pairs are searched. This limits the scope of the proposed approach on mining more general temporal association rules (as a well established concept), and needs to be made more explicit in the paper.
	* The analogy between the proposed approach to Noether's theorem is cannot be considered as "isomorphic" (p2, contribution 3) unless it is proven that the condition of the Noether's theorem is satisfied. Also, after established connection, no further implication (i.e., so what) is drawn, which renders this analogy being just "nice to have".
	* The actually used embedding based method is NE-A which is distant from originally motivated NE-O (no conceptual nor empirical comparison provided). The objective function of NE-A in appendix B.4 is a standard contrastive loss (see e.g., TeRo Xu. et al. [3]), and the regularizer is drawn from TNTComplEX. Thus NE-A, the actually used embedding method, has limited novelty.
	* As a common practice on pattern mining community [4], the approximation ratio of an approximation algorithm is often studied theoretically. Providing theoretical guarantee of the proposed NE-A could strengthen the novelty of the paper.

* **[quality] The empirical evaluation is rather not well justified, strong baselines/settings are missing**.
	* Justification for the presented parameters and thresholds is missing.The hyperparameters of training the embedding is presented as is and without justification (e.g., tuned over grid, used from other papers and why?). Convergence criteria of the embedding training is also not discussed. Thresholds of confidence and support (in section 6.3) are presented as is without justification. 
	* There is no empirical evidence provided to support NE-O being less efficient than NE-A, also no evaluation for NE-O's performance is provided. 
	* In the experiment, only TNTComplEX is used as a non-trivial baseline, however there are many embedding based temporal knowledge graph link prediction/completion methods (e.g., [1, 3]). The main idea of these approach is mapping the quadruples that are similar and adjacent in time on to similar embeddings. Thus, these methods are potentially strong baselines as their embeddings can be used for temporal association search. Moreover, the similarity measure used for TNTComplEX in the empirical evaluation is defined as the product of quadruple scores. Would the accuracy of TNTComplEX improve if it uses the same similarity measure as defined in Eq. 11 and subsequently section 5.2?

### References
* [1] Lacroix et al., Tensor Decompositions for temporal knowledge base completion, ICLR 2020.
* [2] Namaki et al., Discovering Graph Temporal Association Rules, CIKM 2017.
* [3] Xu et al., TeRo: A Time-aware Knowledge Graph Embedding via Temporal Rotation, ACL 2020.
* [4] Cheng et al., A Survey on Algorithms for Mining Frequent Itemsets over Data Streams, KIS 2008.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Please see the clarification in Strength and Weakness.

For reproducibility, code are provided, however the instruction of reproduce the experiments (e.g., Figure 4) are not provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: Based on the aforementioned assessment, I recommend a rejection on this paper.

content.comment:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer for spending valuable time reviewing our manuscript and providing insightful comments. Noticing that the previously poor presentation has strongly misled the reviewer from understanding the genuine novelty of Noether Embeddings, we have substantially revised the expressions in the article. We further improved our work to a large extent with the guide of the reviewer’s comments.

## Major Improvements
1. We have clarified the presentations in the manuscript.
2. We have extended NE for querying event pairs of arbitrary event types, have given a more general version of the theoretical proof, and have conducted relevant experiments.
3. We have further proposed a general heuristic embedding construction procedure with Noether’s theorem.
4. We have developed a unified NE, which is both theoretically provable and experimentally efficient, and have renewed relevant experiments.
5. We have conducted experiments with three more non-trivial TKG baselines (including TeRo Xu. Et al. [1]) to show the necessity of our embedding model.
6. We have extended an online TAM experiment to demonstrate the practicality and potential of our method further.

## Novelty of significance
1. Embedding. We develop an embedding model NE of structured events that naturally encodes the time translation symmetry of TAs, and can efficiently decode conserved quantities to query TAs.
2. Mining. We develop a TAM framework that (1) supports efficient query of an approximate probability distribution of the relative time points within an arbitrary queried range of a potential TA, and (2) rearranges the major time complexity of TAM into the encoding stage, where the training time of NE can be ignored as long as it is shorter than the update period of the event stream.
3. Noether. We develop a heuristic embedding construction procedure, where axiomatized physical systems that satisfy Noether’s theorem can aid the discovery of regularities with general symmetries.


## Key technical innovation (why NE works)
The key technical innovation of NE is the specific use of a global rotating complex vector $r(t)$ for an EFFICIENT cross-correlation-like query of temporal associations by encoding the time translation symmetry of TAs. In the encoding process, $r(t)$ conducts a Fourier expansion for a series of the event embeddings $q(t)=u \circ r(t)$ of each event type while training. The decoding process (calculating $g(\tau)$) only requires a RELATIVE time range ($\tau\in T_r$), regardless of the absolute time of relevant events across time($t\in T_a$). This is caused by the fact that $g(\tau)=||u_c-u_e \circ r(\tau)||=||u_c \circ r(t)-u_e \circ r(t+\tau)||=||q_c(t)-q_e(t+\tau)||$ for any $t$. Relevant event pairs across time (‘for any $t$’) are therefore automatically ‘gathered’ and ‘averaged’ when learning each event embeddings to form the same $g(\tau)$, due to the time translation symmetry of TAs introduced by $r(t)$. This enables TAQ to be conducted efficiently by calculating $g(\tau)$ in minor time complexity. 

## Illustration of the mining framework
1. Encoding. The inputs are structured events, such as (s,p,o,t) quadruples. The
outputs are complex vectors, including entities, predicates, and a global time vector of $\omega$. The encoding process can be implemented in batches or streams, because the most minor component of a training loss is only relevant to the specific information of a single event. The event embeddings, score function, and loss function are concerned in the encoding stage.

2. Decoding. The inputs are trained complex vectors and TA queries of
$(s,o,p_c,p_e)$. The outputs are decoding results, computed by the decoding function $g(\tau)$ and further redistributed by the converting function $p(\tau)$ to form an approximate probability distribution of relative time. $\tau$ is traversed in an arbitrary queried range of relative time points, such as $\tau \in T_r=\\{0,1,2,…,30\\}$, which can be different from the collection of absolute time points, such as $t \in T_a=\{0,1,…,365\}$. The maximum of $p(\tau)$ is then derived. Note that no training is included in this process, which only requires inference of trained vectors. The decoding and converting functions are concerned in the decoding stage.

3. Selecting. The inputs are the decoding results of each TA query. The outputs are 
the judgement of each TA query. A global threshold $p_{th}$ is set, compared with the maximum of $p(\tau)$ for judgements. Once the maximum exceeds $p_{th}$, a TA is justified as exists and the corresponding $\tau$ that maximizes $p(\tau)$ is selected. Computations in this stage are conducted one by one for a fair comparison with Search.


## References
[1] Xu et al., TeRo: A Time-aware Knowledge Graph Embedding via Temporal Rotation, ACL 2020.

[2] Namaki et al., Discovering Graph Temporal Association Rules, CIKM 2017.

content.comment:
## Point-to-Point Responses
### Clarity
> Q1: In section 4, decoding phase, only the similarity measure (Eq. 11) is introduced, but no search procedure is mentioned (e.g. could be similar to Algorithm 1, yet perhaps using kNN search instead).

A1: In the decoding phase of our experiments, all potential TAs are queried one by one as in Algorithm 1 for a fair comparison.

> Q2: Also the embeddings learned according to Eq. 9 and Eq. 11 are potentially not capable of encoding the temporal order (as they are ignored in function h)

A2: (1) Only Eq. 9 is used for learning NE in the encoding process. 
(2) Eq. 11 (Eq.12 in the latest version) is a decoding function for each TAQ. For example, for a TA query $(s,o,p_c,p_e)$, we can derive its decoding results by calculating $g(\tau;s,o,p_c,p_e)$, where $\tau$ is traversed in a relative time range such as $\tau \in T_r=\\{0,1,2,…,30\\}$. 
(3) The temporal information of each quadruple is encoded mainly in a global time vector $\omega$, and also in the complex vectors of each entity and predicate. Temporal order is encoded as a joint consequence of negative sampling and Fourier expansions in the event encoding process.

> Q3: Eq. 9, function h only depends on s and o (why not p or r(t)) is not motivated

A3: Function h was previously set as the function of s and o only for training convergence considerations. In the latest version of NE, we change h to two different constants, either for positive or negative samples for simplicity.

> Q4: Above Eq. 6, notation X(q,t) and Φ(q,t) are not defined.

A4: $\epsilon X(q,t)$ and $\epsilon\Psi(q,t)$ respectively denote a first-order approximation of $\delta t$ and $\delta q(t)$.

> Q5: Eq. 11, τ is defined as relative interval, however on page 2, the notation T is also referred to as relative interval, could it be the set of all possible relative intervals (as this concepts appeared in Appendix Algorithm 1 and never used in the main text)?

A5: T ($T_r$ in the latest version) is the set of all queried $\tau$s, such as $\\{0,1,2,…,30\\}$.

> Q6: Eq. 10, $\gamma$ is not defined.

A6: $\gamma$ is a constant set for training use. In the latest loss $\gamma$ is not needed.

> Q7: as $\tau$ is an interval, t is a timestamp, it is unclear how to understand condition t→τ. Also under the same reasoning, should the r(t) in Eq. 11 be r(τ)? then r(τ) is also not yet defined

A7: $\tau$ is also a timestamp, but was originally referred to as "relative interval" (now as "relative time") since it indicates the convergence time point of a potential temporal association. $\tau$ is the center point of $\bigtriangleup=[\tau(1-\eta), \tau(1+\eta)]$ in a potential TA.

> Q8: Eq. 13, the upper limit of i is n, which is not defined.

A8: $n$ ($d$ in the latest version) is the dimension of complex vectors, the same as D in the time complexity $O(T_rD)$.

In addition, the constructed action is coherent with the Euler-Lagrange Equation, which determines the evolution of a physical system with conservative forces. Analogizing a zero-mass two-particle system connected by a spring, we therefore deduct from only a constructed action to get meaningful inspirations for constructing Noether Embeddings. We summarize the procedure into 5 processes: (1)construction of action (by analogizing a physical system with similar symmetries); (2)applying Euler-Lagrange Equation; (3)applying transformation of symmetry; (4)combining conclusions from (2) and (3) to derive the conserved quantity and constraints for embedding construction; (5)getting inspirations. The objective function of NE-A in appendix B.4 is a standard contrastive loss (see e.g., TeRo Xu. et al. [1]), and the regularizer is drawn from TNTComplEX. Thus NE-A, the actually used embedding method, has limited novelty

A4: The key technical innovation of NE is the specific use of a global rotating complex vector $r(t)$ for an EFFICIENT cross-correlation-like query of temporal associations by encoding the time translation symmetry of TAs. content.title: Fourth Part of Response
content.comment:
## Point-to-Point Responses
### Quality
> Q1: Justification for the presented parameters and thresholds is missing

A1: For baselines from other papers, we use hyperparameters settings in the corresponding papers. Hyperparameters and thresholds of NE are tuned over grid search. Detailed information can be found in Appendix C.

> Q2: The hyperparameters of training the embedding is presented as is and without justification

A2: Selection of hyperparameters in training follows these principles: 1) achieve the training loss convergence of all embedding models. 2) optimize model's performance to some degree but not pursue the ultimate results through tuning over all possible parameters, since the advantages of our model mainly come from the design itself, which has proven superior over baselines.

> Q3: Convergence criteria of the embedding training is also not discussed

A3: Embedding models are trained until the loss stops gradient descent remarkably. That is when we regarded them as having converged.

> Q4: Thresholds of confidence and support (in section 6.3) are presented as is without justification

A4: These are regarded as the task setting of TAM. $gc \geq 0.7, sp \geq 2$ is a reasonable standard of a TA being “confident” and “reliable”.

> Q5: There is no empirical evidence provided to support NE-O being less efficient than NE-A, also no evaluation for NE-O's performance is provided.

A5: We have developed a single and final NE to replace NE-O and NE-A, which is both theoretically reasonable and experimentally efficient, and have renewed relevant experiments.

> Q6: In the experiment, only TNTComplEX is used as a non-trivial baseline
> 
A6: We have conducted experiments with 3 more non-trivial TKG baselines (including TeRo Xu. Et al. [1]) to show the necessity of our embedding model.

> Q7: ‘Would the accuracy of TNTComplEX improve if it uses the same similarity measure as defined in Eq. 11 and subsequently section 5.2’

A7: No, it would not. Eq.11 works only when event embeddings naturally embed time translation symmetry of absolute time over relative time. NE is nearly the simplest form to achieve this function. 
If (1) positive and sample pairs of classic embedding models are also mapped to two different constants, (2) the output of classic embedding models are directly calculated by a cross-correlation function, then TAQ may also be achieved. The key difference in this circumstance is that the time complexity of computing cross-correlations in such a decoding process is rearranged to the encoding process by NE. Training time in the encoding process can be ignored as long as it is shorter than the update period of the event stream.

## References
[1] Xu et al., TeRo: A Time-aware Knowledge Graph Embedding via Temporal Rotation, ACL 2020.

[2] Namaki et al., Discovering Graph Temporal Association Rules, CIKM 2017.
